summary: Reverse the bits of a 32-bit unsigned integer.
mainInsight: Bit i of the input must become bit 31-i of the output: swap mirrored bit pairs (or build the result by shifting), a two-pointer idea on bit positions.

approaches.name: Swap mirrored bits (two pointers)
approaches.summary: For l, r moving inward, XOR-flip both bits only if they differ.

approaches.name: Divide and conquer masks
approaches.summary: Swap halves, then bytes, nibbles, pairs and single bits with masks.
approaches.interviewRelevance: Optimal; also good for repeated calls with a cache of bytes.

personalSolution.approach: Swap mirrored bits with XOR (two pointers)
personalSolution.notes: Good. Know the shift-build and mask versions too.

promptVariants: What is the pattern behind swapping bit i with bit 31-i?
Which general technique does your solution reuse on bits?
cards.explanation: Mirrored positions are processed from both ends, exactly like reversing an array.

promptVariants: Why do you only flip bits when they differ?
How does XOR-flipping implement a swap of two bits?
cards.answer: If the two bits are equal, swapping changes nothing. If they differ, swapping equals flipping both, and `n ^ (1 << pos)` flips a single bit.
keyPoints: XOR with a one-bit mask flips

promptVariants: Your loop runs 16 times, so reverse bits is ___ time.
cards.explanation: The word size is fixed, so the number of iterations is constant.

promptVariants: If reverseBits is called millions of times, how would you speed it up?
What techniques make reverseBits fast when it is called very many times?
cards.answer: Precompute (cache) the reversal of every byte (256 entries) and combine four lookups, or use the divide-and-conquer mask method (5 steps).

promptVariants: Why does `n = n ^ (1 << l)` followed by `n = n ^ (1 << r)` swap two different bits?
Why do the two XOR-with-mask lines exchange a pair of bits that differ?
cards.code:
while l < r:
    leftBit = (n >> l) & 1
    rightBit = (n >> r) & 1
    if leftBit != rightBit:
        n = n ^ (1 << l)
        n = n ^ (1 << r)
    l += 1
    r -= 1
cards.answer: When the bits differ, one is 0 and the other 1; flipping both exchanges them (0->1 at one position, 1->0 at the other). Each XOR with a single-bit mask toggles exactly that bit.
cards.explanation: Python ints are unbounded, so the fixed 32 positions are explicit.

promptVariants: Why must the loop use 32 positions even when n has fewer significant bits?
What happens to leading zeros in the input?
options: Leading zeros become trailing zeros, so all 32 bits matter
They are dropped, since leading zeros carry no value
They cause an overflow in the signed 32-bit result too
They are irrelevant, since only set bits affect the output
cards.answer: Leading zeros become trailing zeros, so all 32 bits matter
cards.explanation: e.g. n = 1 (bit 0 set) must become 2^31; stopping at the highest set bit would give 1.

incorrectOptionExplanations.They are dropped, since leading zeros ca: That would produce a different (shorter) number.
incorrectOptionExplanations.They are irrelevant, since only set bits: They determine the high bits of the result.
